Q: How to combine csv files in Batch at Windows command prompt? A:

Solution for normal sized CSV

Normally for a reasonable sized CSV file the following trick should work:

>new.csv (
   type file1.csv
   more +1 file2.csv
   more +1 file3.csv
   REM etc.
)

Option +1 means skipping first line of data.

Solution for huge CSV file

However, more is using a buffer so when there are more than 65536 lines in data, it will stop at around 65536th line and shows a prompt, which is not what we want.

So for very large CSV files we can use this alternative:

>new.csv (
    type file1.csv
    findstr /v /b "Header_of_file2_csv" file2.csv
    findstr /v /b "Header_of_file3_csv" file3.csv
    REM more...
)

Option /v means "not matching", option /b means matching from the beginning of line.

Proof that it works

file1.csv:

Col1,Col2,Col3
101,102,103
201,202,203
301,302,303

file2.csv:

Col1,Col2,Col3
401,402,403
501,502,503
601,602,603

file3.csv:

Col1,Col2,Col3
701,702,703
801,802,803
901,902,903

Command:

>new.csv (
    type file1.csv
    findstr /v /b "Col1,Col2,Col3" file2.csv
    findstr /v /b "Col1,Col2,Col3" file3.csv
)

Result from new.csv:

Col1,Col2,Col3
101,102,103
201,202,203
301,302,303
401,402,403
501,502,503
601,602,603
701,702,703
801,802,803
901,902,903

Proof that findstr will not stop at processing 65536th line of text file

If there's a concern findstr might act like more and also stops at 65536th line, we need a large file to prove (that it won't stop).

>hugefile.txt (
    REM 7000 x 10 = 70000 > 65536
    for /l %j in (1,1,7000) do @for /l %i in (0,1,9) do @echo %i
    echo last-line
)
findstr last-line hugefile.txt

findstr should print last-line immediately without delay or even wait for any prompt.

Limitation

The command findstr /v /b pattern file will remove any matching pattern in file from output. So if there's any data row having the exact data as the header, it will also be skipped. For instance:

Col1,Col2,Col3
401,402,403
Col1,Col2,Col3
501,502,503
601,602,603

This is a very rare edge case but user of findstr needs to be aware of that.

Dealing with long header data

Sometimes the CSV file can have quite a long header due to many columns in the file. That makes it hard to repeatedly type them all in the command:

>new.csv (
    type file1.csv
    findstr /v /b "Very_long_header_of_file2_csv" file2.csv
    findstr /v /b "Very_long_header_of_file3_csv" file3.csv
    REM more...
)

In such case, you can simply type the first few columns of the header because we use the /b option to skip those matching from the beginning of each line. Like so:

>new.csv (
    type file1.csv
    findstr /v /b "Col1,Col2,Col3" file2.csv
    findstr /v /b "Col1,Col2,Col3" file3.csv
    REM more...
)

In this example we just use the first 3 columns for matching the header. Just remember we need to choose enough header columns to avoid collision with data row columns.

When in doubt of possible collision, and if we are sure all the CSV files sharing the exact same header, we can use environment variable like so:

set "header=Col1,Col2,Col3,Col4,Col5...."
>new.csv (
    type file1.csv
    findstr /v /b "%header%" file2.csv
    findstr /v /b "%header%" file3.csv
    REM more...
)

And of course even when environment variable is used we can also avoid typing all the header columns, if those columns are too many.

Q: Extract contour path from an image A:

I suggest using my contour extraction library Contrek. I’ll show you how to do it using a Ruby script. Contrek is distributed with a Ruby wrapper, but its core is written in C++; if you prefer, the repository contains examples showing how to implement the same logic in C++.

Your original image was about 256x256 pixels; I downscaled it to make the resulting path easier to visualize on screen. The library has a builtin preview system.

Here is the code. Since you specified that you wanted an 8-connectivity path, you need to set the `connectivity: 8` option. I also set the direction to clockwise.

# initialize source image
png_bitmap = Contrek::Bitmaps::PngBitmap.new("./spec/files/images/8hz1k.png")
# define color, in this case white
color = Contrek::Bitmaps::RgbColor.new(r: 255, g: 255, b: 255, a: 255)
# asks to consider any non white piexel
rgb_matcher = Contrek::Matchers::ValueNotMatcher.new(color.raw)
# polygonfinder extracts the path
polygonfinder = Contrek::Finder::PolygonFinder.new(
  png_bitmap,
  rgb_matcher,
  nil,
  {connectivity: 8, versus: :o, compress: {uniq: true, linear: true}})
result = polygonfinder.process_info
      
# benchmarks
puts result.metadata[:benchmarks].inspect
# render inside window
Contrek::Bitmaps::PngBitmap.to_window(result, zoom: 35, coords: false, font_h: 30)
# access coordinates
puts result.points.inspect

Here is the visual output:

path_on_screen

The path is the one you was asking for i think.

Contrek is well-suited for this task. It does not use the Moore-Neighbor algorithm or other standard methods; I wrote a proprietary algorithm that approaches the problem differently. Furthermore, unlike almost all other libraries performing similar extractions, this one supports multithreaded extraction by splitting the image into tiles and stitching the topology back together. You can find full details on how it works in the README. Here the Repo https://github.com/runout77/contrek

Q: How to extract data from a matrix in Google Sheets when some data does not exactly Match the "Row Headers"? A:

This can be done with just SORTN. The three comparisons can be used directly as sort columns to prioritize rows that meet each minimum dimension, followed by the actual dimensions in ascending order to return the smallest qualifying size.

For example, with the requested dimensions in B22:D22:

=SORTN(
 B3:K20,1,2,
 B3:B20>=B22,0,
 C3:C20>=C22,0,
 D3:D20>=D22,0,
 B3:B20,1,
 C3:C20,1,
 D3:D20,1
)

The first three sort criteria put TRUE values before FALSE, so a row meeting all three conditions:

L >= requested L
W >= requested W
t >= requested t

is sorted ahead of any row that does not.

The final three criteria then sort the qualifying rows by L, W, and t ascending. Since SORTN is limited to one row, the result is the smallest available size that satisfies all three requirements.

For example, an input of 8.5, 4.0, 2.5 returns the row for 10, 4.8, 3.

If the desired grade/price column is already known, the same SORTN can return just that value. Only its first argument needs to change. For example, if the grade letter is in B29 and the grade headers are in E1:K1:

=SORTN(
 INDEX(E3:K20,,XMATCH(B29,E1:K1)),1,2,
 B3:B20>=B22,0,
 C3:C20>=C22,0,
 D3:D20>=D22,0,
 B3:B20,1,
 C3:C20,1,
 D3:D20,1
)

So the same sorting logic can be used regardless of which grade column is being returned.

Q: Touch -ar inconsistent behaviour A:

This is a race condition, not a logic bug in your script.

The -ar line isn't actually redundant, which is probably the confusing part. On APFS, touch can't set the creation date directly, but there's a well-known side effect: if you set a file's modification time to something earlier than its current creation date, the OS quietly pulls the creation date back to match. That's the whole trick behind your two-liner touch -r app scpt sets mtime (and atime) to the .app's values, and because that mtime lands earlier than the .scpt's original creation date, macOS backdates the creation date right along with it.

That backdating isn't instant, though. It's the filesystem going back and rewriting the file's metadata after the fact, and that rewrite is what stomps on your access time a moment later. When you type both lines by hand, there's a natural beat between hitting return on line one and line two — enough for that to settle before your -ar call runs. In the script, both lines fire back to back with basically zero delay, so touch -ar can land before the OS has finished whatever it's doing after the first touch, and your access time gets reset to "now" right after the script exits.

Cheapest fix just give it a beat:

#!/bin/zsh
touch -r "$1" "$2"
sleep 1
touch -ar "$1" "$2"

If you're batch-processing a whole folder of these and don't want a flat sleep tax on every single file, verify and retry instead of guessing at a delay:

#!/bin/zsh
touch -r "$1" "$2"
touch -ar "$1" "$2"

ref=$(stat -f %a "$1")
for i in 1 2 3 4 5; do
  [[ "$(stat -f %a "$2")" == "$ref" ]] && break
  sleep 0.3
  touch -ar "$1" "$2"
done

That only sleeps when the race is actually lost, and bails the moment the timestamp sticks so it's fast on the files that don't need retrying.

One thing unrelated to the actual bug: quote your variables, "$1" "$2" instead of bare $1 $2. Won't matter for filenames like yours, but it'll bite you the day one of these paths has a space in it.

Q: Why are the ASCII codes of characters not seen in the dump function output for an object type of varchar2(3885) in a select statement SQL? A:

The 3884 boundary is just where the image plus its header stops fitting in the inline representation. It is an implementation detail and not something to build on. If you want the ASCII codes, dump the attribute instead of the object, like below:

with t as (select mytype_1__('A') o from dual)
select dump(t.o.c1) from t;

That gives you Typ=1 Len=1: 65 as expected, and it works the same for both types since you are now dumping a real varchar2.

Q: Convert TailwindCSS to native CSS? A:

Paste your html code in tailwind-playground

You can access the css in the generated css files tab.

Example

According to tailwind-css docs

Tailwind automatically injects these styles when you include @tailwind base in your CSS (the first 552 lines of generated CSS)

You can remove those base classes by setting preflight = false in tailwind.config.cs

module.exports = {
  corePlugins: {
    preflight: false,
  }
}
